## The idea

A six-note phrase is enough to expose the boundary between score and instrument. The pitches and timings can stay fixed while the synth changes around them. I use that separation throughout the book: the phrase describes what happens, while `use_synth` chooses the machine that makes it audible. Start with `:pluck`, whose sharp attack makes every onset easy to locate. The program stores the phrase as note symbols and gives each note half a beat. `play_phrase` receives those two inputs and renders them in order.

Listen once for event placement, then again for colour and decay. Holding most variables fixed is what turns the example into an experiment. If two edits happen together, the cause of the audible change becomes unclear. The bounded changes below preserve that discipline.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

notes = [:e3, :g3, :a3, :b3, :a3, :e3]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |pitches, lengths|
  pitches.zip(lengths).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

play_phrase notes, durations
```

You hear six evenly spaced notes rise, turn, and settle. The plucked attack makes the rhythm plain, while the final note hangs long enough to sound like an ending.

## Change one thing

1. Replace `:pluck` with `:prophet`. Listen for the softened attack and broad tail; the same six starts become less percussive.

2. Run the phrase with `:blade`, then `:fm`. Compare how clearly you can locate each onset while the notes and sleeps remain fixed.

3. Change the final duration from `1` to `0.5`. The pitch still resolves, though the phrase loses some of its closing weight.

After each edit, restore the original before trying the next one. This keeps the comparisons independent. Write one sentence about the change in onset, duration, register, roughness, or direction. Avoid broad judgements such as “better”; name the feature that moved.

## Why it works

The note array is score data. The helper is a renderer, and the synth selection is configuration. Keeping those roles separate means one edit can recolour the whole phrase without changing its contour or timing.

The program keeps musical material as data until the last possible moment. That separation makes the explanation inspectable: you can print the score, calculate a property, and pass the same values to a renderer. Sound then acts as another view of the data. When the result differs from the calculation, check whether the mismatch comes from the representation, the scheduling, or the synth envelope.

The six-note limit keeps the first program small enough to read from top to bottom. `play` starts an event; `sleep` moves the musical clock; `use_synth` selects a sound generator. Press Run after each single-word synth edit and watch the log pane at the same time. A misspelled synth produces an error rather than a partial performance, and the line number is part of the feedback. Once this score-versus-renderer split is audible, Lesson 2 can replace note names with integers without changing the basic playback loop.

One further comparison separates articulation from instrument choice. Keep `:pluck` and change `release` from `duration * 0.8` to `duration * 1.4`. The notes begin at the same moments, yet their tails overlap. That edit belongs to the renderer rather than the pitch array, so it demonstrates why sound settings should not be hidden inside the score data.

## Take it further

Add a fourth synth choice and a second six-note phrase. Keep one `use_synth` line and one call to `play_phrase`, so changing a single symbol still replaces the instrument. Use the log pane to record the synth and any error message produced by a deliberate misspelling.

The finished file should contain two phrases, four working synth symbols, and one recorded error message with its corrected line. Audition every synth choice in Sonic Pi 5 before deciding which register suits it.
